body.v: Three colleagues finished Lesson 1 this week. The full digest is waiting in the ThisIsTea app, to read whenever you like.

hotspots.explain: The domain is exactly thisistea.example, with nothing added.
No password, no deadline, no pressure.
thisistea.example sits just before the first slash: the link is genuine. You can still skip it and go through the app.
The email lets you read the digest in the app, whenever you like.

who.prompt: Who is really writing to you? Read the address, not just the name.
who.answer: ThisIsTea, from its exact domain: thisistea.example.

emotion.prompt: Which feeling is this email pressing on?

ask.prompt: What does it actually want you to do?
ask.answer: Nothing, apart from reading a digest if you're interested. No password, no payment, no pressure.
choices: Sign in to keep your password
Nothing, apart from reading a digest

verify.prompt: How can you check through a channel you control?
verify.answer: Even with a genuine email, you can leave the link and open the ThisIsTea app yourself.
choices: Reply to ask for a more detailed digest
Forward it to the IT team

actions.label: Open the ThisIsTea app yourself and read the digest
actions.consequence: The same digest is waiting for you there.

actions.label: Click the link to read the digest
actions.consequence: It leads to the real domain, so no harm done. Going through the app is still the better habit.

actions.label: Report it to the IT team as a suspicious email
actions.consequence: The IT team thanks you and confirms the email is genuine. Checking is never a mistake; this one just happened to be fine.

attacker_reveal: I didn't touch this one: thisistea.example without a single extra letter, and nothing to do but read. A link isn't suspicious in itself. What counts is who owns the domain and what it asks of you.
